<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{thm:continuous-elimination}
Assume that $D$ generates a strongly continuous semigroup on $\mathcal H_Q$.  Every mild solution of \eqref{eq:continuous-full} satisfies
\begin{align}
\dot p(t)
={}&Ap(t)+\int_0^tK(t-s)p(s)\,\mathrm d s+\eta(t),
\label{eq:continuous-reduced}\\
K(t)={}&Be^{tD}C,
\label{eq:continuous-kernel}\\
\eta(t)={}&f_P(t)+Be^{tD}q_0+
\int_0^tBe^{(t-s)D}f_Q(s)\,\mathrm d s.
\label{eq:continuous-orthogonal}
\end{align}
Conversely, if $p$ solves \eqref{eq:continuous-reduced} and
\[
q(t)=e^{tD}q_0+
\int_0^te^{(t-s)D}\bigl(Cp(s)+f_Q(s)\bigr)\,\mathrm d s,
\]
then $(p,q)$ solves \eqref{eq:continuous-full}.
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
Variation of constants in the hidden equation gives the displayed expression for $q$.  Substitution into $\dot p=Ap+Bq+f_P$ yields \eqref{eq:continuous-reduced}--\eqref{eq:continuous-orthogonal}; the converse is direct.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
\label{thm:discrete-elimination}
For every $n\ge0$,
\begin{align}
q_n={}&D^nq_0+
\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}D^{n-1-j}\bigl(Cp_j+u_{Q,j}\bigr),
\label{eq:q-elim}\\
p_{n+1}={}&Ap_n+
\sum_{\ell=1}^{n}K_\ell p_{n-\ell}+\eta_n,
\label{eq:discrete-volterra}
\end{align}
where
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:discrete-kernel}
K_\ell=BD^{\ell-1}C,
\qquad \ell\ge1,
\end{equation}
and
\[
\eta_n=u_{P,n}+BD^nq_0+
\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}BD^{n-1-j}u_{Q,j}.
\]
Thus every finite-dimensional hidden block generates an exact matrix-valued Volterra equation.
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
Equation \eqref{eq:q-elim} follows by induction.  Insert it into $p_{n+1}=Ap_n+Bq_n+u_{P,n}$ and reindex.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- definition-1: body_md -->
\label{def:memory-types}
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
\item A \emph{realized memory contribution} is the path-dependent value
\[
\mathfrak m_n^{\mathrm{real}}
=\sum_{\ell=1}^{n}K_\ell p_{n-\ell}.
\]
\item If $\rho(D)<1$, the \emph{structural static return} is
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:static-return}
\mathcal N_0=B(I-D)^{-1}C=\sum_{\ell\ge1}K_\ell.
\end{equation}
\item The \emph{finite-horizon projected-memory correction} is
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:dynamic-memory}
\mathcal M_h=PJ^hP-A^h.
\end{equation}
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end definition-1 -->
<!-- theorem-3: body_md -->
\label{thm:finite-lift}
Suppose
\[
K(t)=\sum_{m=1}^MB_me^{tD_m}C_m.
\]
Define
\[
z_m(t)=\int_0^te^{(t-s)D_m}C_mp(s)\,\mathrm d s.
\]
Then the Volterra equation
\[
\dot p=Ap+\int_0^tK(t-s)p(s)\,\mathrm d s+f
\]
is equivalent in its resolved component to
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:finite-lift}
\dot p=Ap+\sum_{m=1}^MB_mz_m+f,
\qquad
\dot z_m=D_mz_m+C_mp,
\qquad z_m(0)=0.
\end{equation}
<!-- end theorem-3 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
Differentiate the definition of $z_m$ and use $\sum_mB_mz_m=(K*p)(t)$.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- theorem-4: body_md -->
\label{thm:diffusive-lift}
For $K(t)=Bk(t)C$, assume the displayed Bochner integrals are finite.  The continuum system
\begin{align}
\dot p(t)&=Ap(t)+B\int_0^\infty z(\lambda,t)\mu(\,\mathrm d\lambda)+f(t),\\
\partial_tz(\lambda,t)&=-\lambda z(\lambda,t)+Cp(t),
\qquad z(\lambda,0)=0,
\end{align}
is an exact Markovian realization of
\[
\dot p=Ap+B\int_0^tk(t-s)Cp(s)\,\mathrm d s+f.
\]
<!-- end theorem-4 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
Solve the linear equation for $z(\lambda,t)$ and apply Tonelli's theorem to exchange the time and $\lambda$ integrals.  The inner integral is \eqref{eq:bernstein}.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- corollary-1: body_md -->
\label{cor:fractional}
For $0<\alpha<1$,
\[
k_\alpha(t)=\frac{t^{-\alpha}}{\Gamma(1-\alpha)}
=\frac{\sin(\pi\alpha)}{\pi}
\int_0^\infty e^{-\lambda t}\lambda^{\alpha-1}\,\mathrm d\lambda.
\]
Thus fractional Volterra memory is an infinite positive Markovian lift.  Tempering by $e^{-\tau t}$ shifts the relaxation spectrum from $\lambda$ to $\lambda+\tau$.
<!-- end corollary-1 -->
<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
A fractional kernel encodes a particular relaxation spectrum.  Projection alone implies a Volterra kernel, not a power law.  Fractionality must be justified by kernel identification, asymptotics, or a physical mechanism.  The AMOC application below does not make such a claim.
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- theorem-5: body_md -->
\label{thm:kernel-perturbation}
Let $p$ and $p_M$ solve the same linear Volterra initial-value problem on $[0,T]$ with kernels $K$ and $K_M$.  Put
\[
\varepsilon_M=\left\lVert K-K_M\right\rVert_{L^1(0,T)},
\qquad
M_T=\sup_{0\le t\le T}\left\lVert p_M(t)\right\rVert.
\]
Then
\[
\sup_{0\le t\le T}\left\lVert p(t)-p_M(t)\right\rVert
\le
T\varepsilon_MM_T
\exp\!\left[T\bigl(\left\lVert A\right\rVert+\left\lVert K\right\rVert_{L^1(0,T)}\bigr)\right].
\]
<!-- end theorem-5 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
For $e=p-p_M$,
\[
\dot e=Ae+K*e+(K-K_M)*p_M.
\]
Integrate, use Fubini and the $L^1$ kernel bound, and apply Gronwall's inequality.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- theorem-6: body_md -->
\label{thm:schur-factor}
Let
\[
J=\begin{pmatrix}A&B\\C&D\end{pmatrix}
\]
act on $\mathcal H_P\oplus\mathcal H_Q$.  For $z\in\rho(D)$ define
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:Phi}
\Phi(z)=zI_{\mathcal H_P}-A-B(zI_{\mathcal H_Q}-D)^{-1}C.
\end{equation}
Then $zI-J$ is invertible if and only if $\Phi(z)$ is invertible.  In finite dimensions,
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:det-factor}
\det(zI-J)=\det(zI-D)\det\Phi(z).
\end{equation}
When both factors are invertible,
\begin{align}
(zI-J)^{-1}_{PP}&=\Phi(z)^{-1},
\label{eq:resolved-resolvent}\\
(zI-J)^{-1}_{PQ}&=\Phi(z)^{-1}B(zI-D)^{-1}.
\end{align}
<!-- end theorem-6 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
Apply block Gaussian elimination to $zI-J$.  The $PP$ Schur complement is \eqref{eq:Phi}; inversion of the triangular factors gives the stated blocks.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- corollary-2: body_md -->
\label{cor:schur-stability}
Assume $\rho(D)<1$.  Then $J$ is Schur stable if and only if $\Phi(z)$ is invertible for every $|z|\ge1$.
<!-- end corollary-2 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
The hidden factor has no zeros for $|z|\ge1$.  The conclusion follows from \eqref{eq:det-factor}.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- definition-2: body_md -->
If $J$ and $D$ are Schur stable, define
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:resolvent-response}
\mathcal R_\Phi=
\max_{|z|=1}\left\lVert \Phi(z)^{-1}\right\rVert,
\qquad
 d_\Phi=
\min_{|z|=1}\sigma_{\min}(\Phi(z)).
\end{equation}
In the Euclidean metric, $\mathcal R_\Phi=d_\Phi^{-1}$.
<!-- end definition-2 -->
<!-- theorem-7: body_md -->
\label{thm:resolved-recurrence}
The blocks satisfy $X_0=I$, $Y_0=0$ and
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:resolved-recurrence}
X_{h+1}=AX_h+
\sum_{j=0}^{h-1}BD^{h-1-j}CX_j.
\end{equation}
Consequently, $X_h-A^h$ is exactly the sum of paths that leave the resolved space and return within $h$ steps.
<!-- end theorem-7 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
Block multiplication gives $X_{h+1}=AX_h+BY_h$ and $Y_{h+1}=CX_h+DY_h$.  Solve the second recurrence and substitute into the first.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- definition-3: body_md -->
For $H\ge1$ define
\begin{align}
\mathcal G_H&=\max_{1\le h\le H}\left\lVert J^h\right\rVert,\\
\mathcal E_H&=\max_{1\le h\le H}
\bigl(\left\lVert J^h\right\rVert-\rho(J)^h\bigr),\\
\mathcal H_H&=\max_{1\le h\le H}\left\lVert PJ^hQ\right\rVert,\\
\mathcal M_H&=\max_{1\le h\le H}\left\lVert PJ^hP-A^h\right\rVert.
\end{align}
They measure total gain, excess over the modal lower bound, hidden-to-observed transfer, and projected-memory correction, respectively.
<!-- end definition-3 -->
<!-- theorem-8: body_md -->
\label{thm:decoder-oracle}
Consider two forecasts generated by the same $J$, forcing, and resolved initial condition, but initialized with hidden states $q_0$ and $\widehat q_0$.  Then
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:decoder-oracle}
\widehat p_h^{\,\mathrm{dec}}-
\widehat p_h^{\,\mathrm{orc}}
=PJ^hQ(\widehat q_0-q_0).
\end{equation}
In particular,
\[
\left\lVert \widehat p_h^{\,\mathrm{dec}}-
\widehat p_h^{\,\mathrm{orc}}\right\rVert
\le \left\lVert PJ^hQ\right\rVert\,\left\lVert \widehat q_0-q_0\right\rVert.
\]
<!-- end theorem-8 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
Subtract the two full-state recursions.  The initial difference lies in $\mathcal H_Q$ and evolves as $J^hQ(\widehat q_0-q_0)$.  Project with $P$.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- theorem-9: body_md -->
\label{thm:metric}
For every $h\ge0$,
\[
\left\lVert J^h\right\rVert_G=\left\lVert RJ^hR^{-1}\right\rVert_2.
\]
The spectrum is unchanged by the similarity $J\mapsto RJR^{-1}$.  For two metrics $G_1,G_2$ and $S=R_2R_1^{-1}$,
\[
\kappa_2(S)^{-1}\left\lVert J^h\right\rVert_{G_1}
\le
\left\lVert J^h\right\rVert_{G_2}
\le
\kappa_2(S)\left\lVert J^h\right\rVert_{G_1}.
\]
The corresponding bounds hold for physically matched hidden-to-observed maps.
<!-- end theorem-9 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
Change variables with $R$.  The comparison follows from
$R_2J^hR_2^{-1}=S(R_1J^hR_1^{-1})S^{-1}$.
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- assumption-1: body_md -->
\label{ass:critical-mode}
As $\varepsilon\downarrow0$:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
\item $J_\varepsilon$ has a simple real eigenvalue $r_\varepsilon\in(0,1)$ with $r_\varepsilon\to1$;
\item its spectral projector is $\Pi_\varepsilon=v_\varepsilon w_\varepsilon^*$, normalized by $w_\varepsilon^*v_\varepsilon=1$;
\item $J_\varepsilon=r_\varepsilon\Pi_\varepsilon+N_\varepsilon$, with $\Pi_\varepsilon N_\varepsilon=N_\varepsilon\Pi_\varepsilon=0$ and
\[
\left\lVert N_\varepsilon^k\right\rVert\le C\gamma^k,
\qquad 0<\gamma<1,
\]
uniformly in $\varepsilon$;
\item $\left\lVert v_\varepsilon\right\rVert$, $\left\lVert w_\varepsilon\right\rVert$, and $\left\lVert \Sigma_\varepsilon\right\rVert$ are uniformly bounded;
\item the mode is observed and excited:
\[
\left\lvert c_\varepsilon^*v_\varepsilon\right\rvert\ge c_0>0,
\qquad
w_\varepsilon^*\Sigma_\varepsilon w_\varepsilon\ge q_0>0.
\]
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end assumption-1 -->
<!-- theorem-10: body_md -->
\label{thm:scalar-ews}
Under \cref{ass:critical-mode}, the stationary covariance $\Gamma_\varepsilon$ exists and
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:cov-asymptotic}
\Gamma_\varepsilon=
\frac{q_\varepsilon}{1-r_\varepsilon^2}
 v_\varepsilon v_\varepsilon^*+R_\varepsilon,
\qquad
q_\varepsilon=w_\varepsilon^*\Sigma_\varepsilon w_\varepsilon,
\qquad
\sup_\varepsilon\left\lVert R_\varepsilon\right\rVert<\infty.
\end{equation}
Consequently,
\begin{align}
\operatorname{Var}(y_n)
&=
\frac{q_\varepsilon\left\lvert c_\varepsilon^*v_\varepsilon\right\rvert^2}{1-r_\varepsilon^2}+O(1),
\label{eq:var-asymptotic}\\
\operatorname{Corr}(y_{n+1},y_n)
&=r_\varepsilon+O(1-r_\varepsilon^2)
\longrightarrow1.
\label{eq:ac-asymptotic}
\end{align}
<!-- end theorem-10 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
The stationary covariance is
\[
\Gamma_\varepsilon=\sum_{k\ge0}J_\varepsilon^k\Sigma_\varepsilon(J_\varepsilon^*)^k.
\]
Since $J_\varepsilon^k=r_\varepsilon^k\Pi_\varepsilon+N_\varepsilon^k$, the projector--projector term equals
\[
\sum_{k\ge0}r_\varepsilon^{2k}\Pi_\varepsilon\Sigma_\varepsilon\Pi_\varepsilon^*
=
\frac{q_\varepsilon}{1-r_\varepsilon^2}v_\varepsilon v_\varepsilon^*.
\]
The two cross terms are uniformly bounded by a geometric series in $r_\varepsilon\gamma$, and the $N_\varepsilon$--$N_\varepsilon$ term by a geometric series in $\gamma^2$.  This proves \eqref{eq:cov-asymptotic} and \eqref{eq:var-asymptotic}.  The lag-one covariance has leading term
$r_\varepsilon q_\varepsilon\left\lvert c_\varepsilon^*v_\varepsilon\right\rvert^2/(1-r_\varepsilon^2)$ and a uniformly bounded remainder; division by \eqref{eq:var-asymptotic} gives \eqref{eq:ac-asymptotic}.
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- remark-2: body_md -->
The theorem requires more than $\rho(J_\varepsilon)\to1$.  The critical mode must be simple, separated from faster modes, not rendered ill conditioned by a diverging eigenbasis, visible in the chosen scalar, and excited by the stochastic forcing.  These are precisely the assumptions that projection can violate.
<!-- end remark-2 -->
<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
\label{prop:oscillatory}
Consider the normal two-dimensional block
\[
J_r=r
\begin{pmatrix}
\cos\omega&-\sin\omega\\
\sin\omega&\cos\omega
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad 0<r<1,
\]
with isotropic noise and any nonzero scalar coordinate observation.  Then stationary variance diverges as $(1-r^2)^{-1}$, but
\[
\operatorname{Corr}(y_{n+1},y_n)=r\cos\omega
\longrightarrow\cos\omega.
\]
Unless $\omega=0$, lag-one correlation does not approach one.
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
The stationary covariance is a scalar multiple of the identity.  The one-step covariance in any coordinate is therefore $r\cos\omega$ times the variance.
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- proposition-2: body_md -->
\label{prop:invisible}
In \cref{thm:scalar-ews}, if $c_\varepsilon^*v_\varepsilon=0$, the leading divergent covariance component is absent from $y_n$.  If $w_\varepsilon^*\Sigma_\varepsilon w_\varepsilon=0$, the critical mode is not stochastically excited.  In either case, scalar variance need not diverge although $r_\varepsilon\to1$.
<!-- end proposition-2 -->
<!-- proof-13: body_md -->
Both statements follow directly from the coefficient of the singular term in \eqref{eq:var-asymptotic}.  Explicit diagonal examples show that the remaining variance can stay bounded.
<!-- end proof-13 -->
<!-- theorem-11: body_md -->
\label{thm:nonnormal-counterexample}
Fix $a,b\in(-1,1)$ with $a\ne b$ and define
\[
J_\kappa=
\begin{pmatrix}
a&\kappa\\0&b
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
\Sigma=
\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
y_n=e_1^*x_n.
\]
Then $\rho(J_\kappa)=\max\{|a|,|b|\}<1$ for every $\kappa$, while the stationary scalar variance is
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:nonnormal-var}
\operatorname{Var}(y_n)=
\frac{\kappa^2}{(a-b)^2}
\left(
\frac{1}{1-a^2}
+
\frac{1}{1-b^2}
-
\frac{2}{1-ab}
\right).
\end{equation}
Hence $\operatorname{Var}(y_n)\to\infty$ as $|\kappa|\to\infty$ although the spectrum remains fixed and uniformly stable.
<!-- end theorem-11 -->
<!-- proof-14: body_md -->
For $k\ge0$,
\[
(J_\kappa^k)_{12}
=\kappa\frac{a^k-b^k}{a-b}.
\]
Only noise in the second coordinate reaches $y$.  Summing the squared impulse response over $k$ gives \eqref{eq:nonnormal-var}.
<!-- end proof-14 -->
<!-- proposition-3: body_md -->
\label{prop:turning-point}
Let $J$ be any fixed Schur-stable matrix, let $x_{n+1}=Jx_n+\xi_{n+1}$, and define a scalar observable
\[
s_n=m(\lambda_n)+c^*x_n,
\]
where $m$ is differentiable and $m'(\lambda_*)=0$.  Then the mean scalar response has a turning point at $\lambda_*$, while the spectral stability of $J$ is unchanged.  Therefore
\[
\frac{\,\mathrm d}{\,\mathrm d\lambda}\mathbb E s=0
\quad\not\Rightarrow\quad
\rho(J)=1.
\]
Conversely, there are families $J_\lambda$ with $\rho(J_\lambda)\uparrow1$ for which the derivative of the observed mean is nonzero.  Hence neither implication holds without additional structural assumptions.
<!-- end proposition-3 -->
<!-- proof-15: body_md -->
For the fixed stable matrix, stationarity gives $\mathbb E x_n=0$ after centering, hence $\mathbb E s_n=m(\lambda_n)$ and the first implication fails at any critical point of $m$.  Conversely, let $J_\lambda=\operatorname{diag}(\lambda,a)$ with $|a|<1$ and $\lambda\uparrow1$, and take $m(\lambda)=\lambda$ with $c=e_2$.  Then the full system approaches a spectral boundary while $\,\mathrm d\mathbb E s/\,\mathrm d\lambda=1$ and the observed coordinate remains uniformly stable.  Thus the reverse implication also fails.
<!-- end proof-15 -->
<!-- proposition-4: body_md -->
\label{prop:delayed-return}
For every integer $H\ge1$ and scalar $\beta\ne0$, there exists a nilpotent, hence Schur-stable, hidden realization $(B,C,D)$ such that
\[
BD^{\ell-1}C=0,
\qquad 1\le\ell\le H,
\]
but
\[
BD^HC=\beta.
\]
Thus two reduced systems can have identical memory coefficients through lag $H$ and differ at lag $H+1$.
<!-- end proposition-4 -->
<!-- proof-16: body_md -->
Let $\mathcal H_Q=\mathbb R^{H+1}$ with basis $e_1,\dots,e_{H+1}$.  Set $C(1)=e_1$, $De_j=e_{j+1}$ for $j\le H$, $De_{H+1}=0$, and $Bz=\beta z_{H+1}$.  Then $D^{\ell-1}e_1=e_\ell$, which is annihilated by $B$ for $\ell\le H$, while $BD^He_1=\beta$.
<!-- end proof-16 -->
<!-- head-1: body_md -->
A gain comparison should not be driven solely by one branch crossing the unit circle.
\item \emph{Test nested observed spaces.}  A scalar may detect susceptibility while a two- or three-dimensional space is needed for closure.
\item \emph{Stress nonstationarity explicitly.}  Affine forcing and an intercept already span linear time on a ramp; quadratic time is a nontrivial additional stress.
\item \emph{Separate description from warning skill.}  Co-movement before a transition is not a validated EWS without chronological out-of-sample testing or independent trajectories.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end head-1 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
Under \cref{ass:critical-mode}, the remainder $R_\varepsilon$ in \eqref{eq:cov-asymptotic} satisfies
\[
\left\lVert R_\varepsilon\right\rVert
\le
\frac{2C_1}{1-\gamma}+
\frac{C_2}{1-\gamma^2}
\]
for constants independent of $\varepsilon$.
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- proof-17: body_md -->
Expand the covariance series into projector--projector, two projector--$N$ cross terms, and the $N$--$N$ term.  Uniform boundedness of $v_\varepsilon,w_\varepsilon,\Sigma_\varepsilon$ bounds the cross terms by $C_1\sum_{k\ge0}(r_\varepsilon\gamma)^k\le C_1/(1-\gamma)$ and the final term by $C_2\sum_{k\ge0}\gamma^{2k}$.
<!-- end proof-17 -->
